recognition and time estimation. The results indicate that the proposed method
achieves a high accuracy of 0.83 for activity recognition and a mean absolute
error of 6.8 seconds in time prediction. Furthermore, the study compares the
performance of the proposed method with existing approaches and highlights its
advantages. The code and pre-trained models for this study are available online.

The widespread adoption of facial recognition technology has led to significant concerns over its potential misuse, particularly in the form of backdoor attacks that can compromise user privacy. These malicious attacks can be triggered by specific inputs, allowing attackers to access sensitive information. In this study, we investigate the threat of backdoor attacks on face identification systems and develop a novel defense mechanism that can detect and prevent such attacks. We introduce ASR2K, a pioneering system that enables speech recognition for approximately 2000 languages, leveraging only text data. This achievement is made possible by a novel approach that utilizes a single, versatile text encoder to generate acoustic embeddings for unseen languages, thereby bridging the gap between languages that share similar alphabets. Our text encoder is trained on a massive 1.4 billion word dataset using a masked language modeling task, and its acoustic capabilities are refined through a self-supervised process. In contrast to prior work, our system does not rely on pre-existing speech recognition models or labeled data, and instead, generates acoustic representations that can be fine-tuned for specific speech recognition tasks. We demonstrate the effectiveness of ASR2K by achieving competitive results on speech recognition benchmarks for three languages, and also showcase its ability to generate coherent audio for 20 languages, even when trained on text data alone. Furthermore, our system outperforms the baseline on 14 out of 20 languages, and in some cases, achieves comparable results. The source code for ASR2K is available on GitHub. Videos and audio samples can be found on YouTube and SoundCloud, respectively. Additionally, our system's audio synthesis capabilities can be experienced through a web demo. Active learning strategies aim to minimize the number of labeled samples required for training by selecting the most informative samples to annotate. Current methods focus on improving the training process by choosing samples that will enhance the model's performance on the training set. However, this approach is flawed because it prioritizes training metrics over test performance. In this paper, we introduce a novel active learning framework that directly boosts test performance. Our approach involves identifying the most informative samples to annotate, which in turn improves the model's test performance. To achieve this, we use a test performance metric that is trained on a subset of the unlabeled data and a small labeled dataset. We then use this metric to select the most informative samples to annotate, which are added to the labeled dataset and used to retrain the model. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach outperforms existing methods on multiple datasets, and we provide theoretical analysis to support our results. This study examines the effectiveness of factor models in predicting mortality rates, with a specific focus on whether incorporating time-dependent factor influences yields better results. We compare the performance of three factor models, each with either time-dependent or time-invariant factor loadings, using data from the United States and the United Kingdom. Our analysis reveals that models incorporating time-dependent factor loadings consistently outperform those assuming fixed factor influences, as measured by the mean squared error of predicted mortality rates. Furthermore, we investigate the practical implications of incorporating time-dependent factor loadings in actuarial applications, such as pricing annuities and determining reserve funds. Our results suggest that using time-dependent factor loadings can lead to more accurate pricing and reserve calculations, although the differences are relatively small. Overall, our findings indicate that incorporating time-dependent factor loadings can provide a more accurate representation of mortality trends and improve the precision of actuarial predictions. However, we also note that the associated increased complexity may not be justified by the relatively small gains in accuracy. Ultimately, we conclude that the choice between using time-dependent factor loadings and a simpler, more traditional approach depends on the specific context and requirements of the actuarial application. A key challenge in reinforcement learning is balancing exploration and exploitation effectively.  To address this issue, we propose a new approach that combines the strengths of model-based and model-free methods.  Our approach involves using a value function model to predict future outcomes and a policy model to determine the best actions, while also incorporating exploration through a random action selection method.  Our method, called MPC-Value, has been shown to outperform both model-based and model-free approaches in a variety of scenarios, particularly in complex environments with sparse rewards.  Our results demonstrate that MPC-Value can achieve higher returns and faster learning times than other methods, and that its performance is particularly strong in environments with sparse rewards. Langevin Monte Carlo is a widely used Markov Chain Monte Carlo method for generating samples from complex probability distributions. Despite its widespread application, a comprehensive understanding of its convergence properties is still incomplete. This study addresses this gap by developing a theory of convergence for Langevin Monte Carlo in the context of non-log-concave probability distributions. By leveraging the concept of weak convexity, a milder condition than strong convexity, we establish a connection between the weak convexity of a probability distribution and the first-order stationarity of Langevin Monte Carlo samples. This connection is used to derive a lower bound on the first-order stationarity of the algorithm's output, which is expressed in terms of the distribution's weak convexity and the number of iterations performed. The study also provides a general framework for analyzing the convergence of Langevin Monte Carlo in the context of non-log-concave probability distributions. This framework is applied to the analysis of the exponential distribution, which is shown to be weakly convex and log-Sobolev regular. The study's results are further illustrated through numerical experiments involving the exponential distribution. The findings of this study are expected to have a significant impact on the development of efficient algorithms for generating samples from complex probability distributions. We examine the conditions under which a mixed graph with a cut vertex will have exactly two positive eigenvalues. Additionally, we provide a characterization of mixed graphs with a spectral radius exceeding 1/2, which also possess exactly two positive eigenvalues. These findings are further extended to mixed graphs with multiple cut vertices. The results are also applicable to directed graphs, which are a subset of mixed graphs featuring only directed edges. The development of deep learning models for document analysis has been hindered by the scarcity of publicly accessible, high-quality training data. The emergence of open-source datasets has significantly contributed to the growth of this field, with the Govdocs1 dataset being a notable example. However, this dataset has several limitations, including its outdated nature and narrow focus on government documents. In response, we present NapierOne, a new dataset comprising 1.5 million contemporary documents from various sources, including invoices, contracts, and financial statements. The dataset is annotated with 10 categories and is suitable for training models to classify and identify specific sections within documents. The performance of leading OCR models on this dataset is evaluated, with the results indicating that NapierOne is a valuable resource for advancing document analysis techniques.
